```{r setup}
library(multiweb)
```

# Overview

The `multiweb` package provides tools for analyzing and comparing ecological networks, particularly food webs and multiplex networks, through a set of reproducible and customizable functions. It allows for the computation of structural and dynamic properties, module detection, species roles, trophic positions, entropy- and centrality-based metrics, structural stability thresholds, and extinction simulations. Multiplex (multilayer) networks are supported throughout, including aggregation, interactive visualization, and 3D layer rendering.

This vignette introduces the general structure of the package and showcases typical usage patterns.

# Data Structure

The `multiweb` package works with an individual network and many functions accept **lists of network objects**, where each network is typically a food web represented by a directed graph. The preferred format is a list of `igraph` objects, where each node is a species and directed edges represent trophic links.

```{r example-net, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
data("netData")  # A list of food web networks included in the package
net <- netData[[23]]
plot_troph_level_ggplot(net)
```
<!-- warning=FALSE is set globally, no change needed here -->

# Basic Metrics

## Global metrics

You can calculate a set of **global network metrics** such as number of species (S), connectance (C), mean trophic level using:

```{r multiple-metrics}
metrics_all <- calc_topological_indices(netData)
head(metrics_all)
```

## Modularity and Communities

Detect modules for a list of networks using any of the algorithms in igraph or **Infomap** (requires the installation of infomap in the system from https://www.mapequation.org/infomap/#Install). By default it uses the cluster_spinglass algorithm from igraph.


```{r modularity}
mod <- calc_modularity(netData,cluster_function = run_infomap)
mod$network_name <- names(netData)
head(mod) 
```

You can visualize the modular structure using:

```{r module-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
mod  <- run_infomap(net)
plot_troph_level_ggplot(net, modules = TRUE, community_obj = mod)
```

# Topological Roles

You can compute species' **topological roles** and plot them: 

```{r roles, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
mod  <- run_infomap(net)
roles <- calc_topological_roles(net, community = mod)
roles_class <- classify_topological_roles(roles, net, community = mod)
head(roles_class$hub_conn)
roles_class$gp
```

# Entropy and Complexity

Quantify network complexity with **singular value decomposition (SVD) entropy**:

```{r entropy}
svd_ent <- calc_svd_entropy(net)
svd_ent
```

This metric is useful for comparing structural complexity across multiple networks.

## Centrality measures

`calc_centrality()` generalizes centrality calculation to any centrality function available in `igraph` (eigenvector centrality, PageRank, betweenness, degree, etc.), returning both a ranked table and a plot of the top species:

```{r centrality, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
cent <- calc_centrality(net, centrality_func = igraph::page_rank)
head(cent$CentralityScores)
cent$Plot_Centrality
```

## Detailed SVD importance

A more detailed decomposition of network complexity is available through `calc_svd_entropy_importance()`, which — in addition to entropy and rank — reports each species' contribution to the dominant singular value (i.e. its structural importance as prey and as predator):

```{r svd-importance, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
svd_imp <- calc_svd_entropy_importance(net)
svd_imp$Entropy
svd_imp$Plot_Prey_Importance
```


# Randomizations and Null Models

The package includes tools for generating **null models** maintaining the degree distribution (Curbe ball algorithm):

```{r nullmodel, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
rand_net <- curve_ball(net)
rand_metrics <- calc_modularity(rand_net, cluster_function = cluster_walktrap)

# Example: show distribution of connectance (C) and empirical value
library(ggplot2)
empirical_m <- calc_modularity(net, cluster_function = cluster_walktrap)$Modularity
ggplot(rand_metrics, aes(x = Modularity)) +
  geom_density(fill = "grey", color = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = empirical_m, color = "salmon", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Modularity in Randomized Networks",
       x = "Modularity")
```

or using the **niche model** to generate random networks with the same size and connectance:

```{r nullmodel1, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}

S <- metrics_all[23,"Size"]
C <- metrics_all[23,"Connectance"]
rand_net <- generate_niche(S,C,nsim=1000)
rand_metrics <- calc_modularity(rand_net, cluster_function = cluster_walktrap)

# Example: show distribution of connectance (C) and empirical value
library(ggplot2)
empirical_m <- calc_modularity(net, cluster_function = cluster_walktrap)$Modularity
ggplot(rand_metrics, aes(x = Modularity)) +
  geom_density(fill = "grey", color = "black") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = empirical_m, color = "salmon", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Modularity in Randomized Networks",
       x = "Modularity")
```

You can then use these null models to assess the significance of observed metrics.


## Calculation of interaction intensity and weighted metrics

Here we calculate interaction intensity using body mass and density data from the Potter Cove food web (data included in the package) and estimate weighted topological indices.

```{r interIntensity}
pc_i <- calc_interaction_intensity(
  PotterCove_bm,
  res_mm = r_bodymass,
  res_den = r_density,
  con_mm = c_bodymass,
  int_dim = D
)

# Build igraph object with weights from interaction strengths
g <- graph_from_data_frame(
  d = pc_i %>% dplyr::select(resource, consumer, weight = qRC),
  directed = TRUE
)

# Now compute weighted indices
calc_weighted_topological_indices(g)
  
```

## Alternative interaction intensity estimation (O'Gorman 2010)

As an alternative to the body-mass/density approach above — useful when resource density data are unavailable — `calc_interaction_intensity2()` estimates interaction strength from predator body mass and the number of resources per consumer, following O'Gorman et al. (2010):

```{r interIntensity2}
edge_list <- tibble::tibble(
  predator = c("A", "A", "B", "C"),
  prey = c("B", "C", "D", "D"),
  predator_mass = c(10, 10, 5, 3)
)

calc_interaction_intensity2(
  edge_list,
  consumer_n = predator,
  resource_n = prey,
  bodymass_n = predator_mass,
  output_format = "edgelist"
)
```

# Using multiplex networks

The package also supports **multiplex networks**, where multiple types of interactions are represented as layers. You can create a multiplex object and compute metrics across layers. 

```{r multiplex}

fpath <- system.file("extdata", package = "multiweb")
dn <- list.files(fpath,pattern = "^Kefi2015.*\\.txt$")
mnet <- readMultiplex(dn,c("Negative","Positive","Antagonistic"),fpath,skipColum=2)

```

You can then compute metrics like modularity for the entire multiplex structure, in this case using the interface to info_map algorithm.

```{r multiplex-metrics, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}

mod_multi <- run_infomap_multi(mnet)
head(mod_multi$communities)

plots <- plot_multiplex_modules(mnet, mod_multi$communities)
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = plots, ncol = 3)
```

Layers sharing the same node set can be combined into a single aggregate network — summing edge weights where interactions coincide across layers — which is useful as a common backbone for layout or as an approximation of overall interaction load. `harmonize_node_sets()` first ensures every layer shares the same set of nodes (adding isolated nodes where needed) before aggregating:

```{r multiplex-aggregate}
mnet_named <- mnet
names(mnet_named) <- c("Negative", "Positive", "Trophic")
mnet_named <- harmonize_node_sets(mnet_named)
agg_net <- aggregate_multiplex_network(mnet_named)
agg_net
```

For a 3D view of all layers stacked together, `plot_multi3D()` (adapted from the `muxViz` project) renders each layer as a semi-transparent plane using `rgl`, optionally with an aggregate layer on top. This opens an interactive OpenGL device, so it is best explored in an active R session rather than rendered here:

```{r multiplex-3d, eval=FALSE}
plot_multi3D(
  g.list = mnet_named,
  layer.colors = RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(3, "Set2"),
  node.colors = "auto",
  node.size.scale = 0.5,
  show.aggregate = TRUE
)
```


# Structural Stability (QSS)

## Estimating the stability threshold

Real food webs must be dynamically stable, which requires some minimal level of intraspecific self-regulation (self-damping). Because the true amount of self-regulation is rarely known, `calc_stability_threshold()` searches for the `selfDamping` value at which a target proportion of simulated community matrices (Jacobians) become unstable — by default, 5% negative-eigenvalue crossings — using [calc_QSS()] internally. Lower (more negative) thresholds indicate networks that require less self-regulation to remain stable:

```{r stability-threshold}
stab <- calc_stability_threshold(net, nsim = 200, ncores = 1, verbose = FALSE)
stab$threshold
```

The search trajectory can be visualized directly:

```{r stability-curve, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
plot_stability_curve(stab)
```

## Extinction simulations

`multiweb` also provides tools to evaluate how the loss of one or more species affects structural stability, by comparing QSS distributions before and after deletion — useful for identifying keystone species or estimating robustness to targeted or random extinctions.

To compare the whole network against the network without a given set of species:

```{r extinction-grp}
sp_sample <- V(net)$name[1:3]
ext_grp <- calc_QSS_extinction_dif_grp(net, sp_sample, nsim = 100, ncores = 1)
head(ext_grp)
```

To simulate an incremental extinction sequence (species removed one at a time, without secondary extinctions):

```{r extinction-seq}
ext_seq <- calc_QSS_extinctions_seq(net, sp_sample, nsim = 100, ncores = 1)
head(ext_seq)
```

Note: `nsim` and `ncores` are set low here for a fast-running vignette; for actual analyses, larger `nsim` (e.g. 1000) and more cores are recommended for stable estimates.


# Interactive Visualization

For exploratory work, `multiweb` provides interactive, draggable network visualizations built on `visNetwork`, as an alternative to the static `ggplot2`/`ggraph` plots shown above. Nodes are still organized by trophic level on the y-axis, but can be dragged, zoomed, searched, and hovered for details.

```{r visnet}
plot_troph_level_visNet(net, modules = TRUE)
```

For multiplex networks, `plot_troph_level_visNet_multi()` overlays all interaction layers on the same trophic-level plot, computing trophic level only from the designated trophic layer, with distinguishable edge colors/styles per layer, an interactive layer filter, and a legend:

```{r visnet-multi}
plot_troph_level_visNet_multi(
  mnet_named,
  trophic_layer = "Trophic",
  layer_dashed = c("Negative", "Positive")
)
```

Note: when knitting to HTML these render as interactive embedded widgets; if the vignette is exported to PDF for external documentation (e.g. as supporting material), interactivity will be lost and a static screenshot may be preferable.
